newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS-French auto sales hit worst June since 1962.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-French auto sales hit worst June since 1962.

text.p: Car sales in France fell 30.7 percent last month, the worst June performance since 1962, as price-cutting failed to entice anxious consumers, industry officials said on Tuesday.
The French carmakers' association CCFA reported sales of new cars sank to 93,212 units in June from 134,489 a year earlier, the sixth consecutive monthly decline.
Stripping out distortions due to the different number of working days, June sales were down 34 percent, it said.
"The market has deteriorated from previous months," the chairman of PSA Peugeot Citroen Jacques Calvet said at a news conference to present a gearbox developed jointly with Renault.
"The only rise we're seeing is in price discounts," Renault chairman Louis Schweitzer said.
The two chairmen said the third quarter would also be difficult, with no recovery expected before November.
French industry officials have cut their forecasts for the year to 1.80 million sales, a 15.6 percent drop from last year, and even that objective looks hard to attain.

The CCFA said the June figures show demand has not recovered from the after-effects of a state rebate scheme which ran out last September after a surge in sales expected to dwarf this year's third-quarter results.
January-June sales fell 23.7 percent to 784,559 units, below first-half 1993 levels when Europe's car industry was in a deep recession, CCFA chairman Yves de Belabre said.

"France is out of step with the rest of Europe. Italy's market is booming, Spain's is coming along well, Britain's market is fine, Germany's market is slightly weaker but is expected to recover," he told reporters.

"Economic surveys showed a pickup in some sectors in the second quarter and we're waiting to see if that spills over into the auto industry," he said. Consumer sentiment relative to the car industry appeared "cautious or anxious", he said.
Renault, General Motors and Fiat reported their sales in France plunged nearly 50 percent in June.

A Renault spokeswoman said the drop in sales -- more than double the 21.1 percent fall in PSA Peugeot Citroen sales -- was due to low inventories in the runup to the new model year begun on Tuesday. She said orders were unchanged from June 1996.
"Our performance was atypical relative to the other car companies. We had less in stock ... after managing inventories to arrive at the end of the model year at very low levels."
The two companies' chairmen were divided on whether they wanted France's new Socialist-led government to set up new incentives to spur car sales.
Renault's Schweitzer said he did not favour measures that would lead to another boom-and-bust cycle, while Calvet said he did favour measures encouraging consumers to trade in clunkers.
They both urged the government not to do anything -- even indirectly through tax policy -- to hurt the industry.

Higher sales in other European countries provided some relief for the French auto makers. Their car exports increased 13 percent in the first five months of 1997 and their share of the European market excluding France climbed to 16 percent in January-May from 15.2 percent.
